demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
He is 52, a South Asian man who has spent most of his adult life doing domestic work in other people’s homes. He describes himself as careful, quiet, and “the sort of person who checks everything twice.” For years, being a maid has suited him. He likes routine: arriving early, sweeping and mopping in a set order, folding clothes sharply, keeping kitchens spotless. He says there is dignity in leaving a place cleaner than he found it. Since his divorce, work has also given shape to long days and a reason to stay moving.

The event that stays with him happens on an ordinary afternoon about two years ago, in an apartment where he has worked for several months. He is cleaning while the employer’s elderly mother rests in the sitting room. He remembers being behind schedule and wanting to finish before the family comes home. In the bathroom, he uses a strong floor cleaner and then takes a call from his brother overseas. He means to go back and dry the floor fully, maybe put a cloth at the doorway, but he is distracted. A few minutes later he hears a sharp cry and then the heavy, unmistakable sound of a body striking the tile.

When he reaches the hallway, the older woman is on the floor, twisted awkwardly, her face pale with pain. He says he knows instantly what has happened, even before he sees the wet shine on the tiles. He calls for help, kneels beside her, and keeps repeating, “I am sorry, I am sorry,” while waiting for the ambulance. At the hospital he learns she has serious injuries—multiple fractures, surgery, a long recovery. No one tells him he intended harm, and the family does not accuse him in the way he fears, but he cannot tolerate the fact that his carelessness is enough.

In the first weeks afterward, he barely sleeps. When he closes his eyes, he hears the cry and the thud again, as if the sound is happening in the room with him. Sometimes he jolts awake with his heart pounding, smelling cleaning solution though his room is dry. During the day he replays the sequence endlessly: the wet floor, the phone call, the steps she must have taken, the second he should have acted differently. He starts saying to himself, “You did this. You ruined her life.” He avoids mirrors because he cannot stand his own face when that thought comes.

Returning to work becomes its own ordeal. He still goes because he needs the income, but now each task is crowded with fear. He wipes floors until they are nearly dry before anyone can cross them. He places warning cloths, then checks them again and again. If someone walks near a recently cleaned area, he feels a surge of panic and watches their feet instead of their face. In kitchens he becomes preoccupied with hazards—knives left out, hot water, loose cords, stools not pushed in. Employers sometimes praise him for being thorough, but they also notice that he moves more slowly and startles when spoken to from behind.

Outside work, his world narrows. He turns down invitations from friends at the mosque because he does not want to answer simple questions about how he is doing. He has always been somewhat reserved, but now he isolates in a more painful way, spending evenings alone in his rented room with the television on low volume, not really watching. His divorced life had already left him with a sense of personal failure; after the accident, that feeling hardens into something harsher. He tells himself that he is unfit to be responsible for anyone or anything. When his adult daughter calls, he keeps conversations short, worried she will hear the strain in his voice and ask more than he can bear to explain.

He also begins avoiding the neighborhood where the accident happened. If a bus route passes that block, he gets off early and walks farther. Seeing elderly women makes him unexpectedly tense, not because they have done anything, but because they bring back the image of the woman on the tile. Sometimes in shops, if he hears a sudden cry from a child or the crash of a dropped object, his whole body reacts before he can think. His shoulders go rigid, his breath turns shallow, and for a moment he is back in that apartment hallway, already too late.

What troubles him most in the present is that time has not softened the event in the way he expected. He still measures days against it: before that afternoon and after. He knows, rationally, that accidents happen, that he did not mean to injure anyone, and that the family eventually stopped contacting him not out of hatred but because life moved on. Yet emotionally he remains fixed at the scene, scanning for danger, bracing for blame, unable to trust his own hands to carry out the work he once did with pride. He says that before, cleaning made a home feel safe. Now every bucket of water feels like a risk he has to survive.
